slides.title: How information retrieval evolved over time?
slides.body:
![[fig-ir-history-convergence|85%]]

***

| **1950** | **1990** | **2010** | **2020** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Retrieve records** | **Rank documents** | **Learn representations** | **Generate responses** |
| Boolean retrieval | BM25, PageRank | [word2vec](https://arxiv.org/abs/1301.3781), BERT | RAG, generative search |

***

- Is generative AI part of information retrieval?
- **What exactly is IR in 2026?**
slides.notes: ⏱ 9:01:30 · 1½ min — Four eras by what could be scored: match, rank, learn vectors, generate over evidence. Land on the two questions; the talk answers them. Skip the individual examples if behind.
slides.summary: history of information retriaval ... and this deck will answer what is IR in 2026? - is genAI used in IR?

slides.title: History of Search, Recommender systems and Conversational AI
slides.body:
<!-- gap -->

| Lineage | Selected papers | Signal added | Scope in cited work |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Classical information retrieval** | [Luhn, 1957](https://doi.org/10.1147/rd.14.0309); Salton, **1968**; [Salton et al., 1975](https://doi.org/10.1145/361219.361220); [BM25, 1994](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/okapi-at-trec-3/) | Term frequency, inverse document frequency, document length | Lexical document–query ranking; no link graph or user model |
| **Web search** | [PageRank, 1998](https://research.google/pubs/the-anatomy-of-a-large-scale-hypertextual-web-search-engine/); [HITS, 1999](https://doi.org/10.1145/324133.324140) | Link structure as authority and hub signals | Ranking web pages from content and links, not individual preferences or dialogue |
| **Recommender systems** | [GroupLens, 1994](https://doi.org/10.1145/192844.192905); [Amazon item-to-item filtering, 2003](https://doi.org/10.1109/MIC.2003.1167344); [matrix factorization, 2009](https://doi.org/10.1109/MC.2009.263) | Ratings, purchases, and user–item interactions | Interaction-based prediction; [Schein et al., 2002](https://doi.org/10.1145/564376.564421) measured the cold-start case |
| **Conversational interfaces** | [ELIZA, 1966](https://doi.org/10.1145/365153.365168) → [seq2seq, 2014](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.3215) → [Transformer, 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762) → [RAG, 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401) | Scripts, learned sequence context, attention, then retrieved evidence | ELIZA matched scripted patterns; seq2seq and Transformer generated from learned context; RAG coupled generation to retrieval |

***

> The cited sequence adds term statistics (**1957–1975**), links (**1998–1999**), user–item behavior (**1994–2009**), learned sequence context (**2014–2017**), and retrieval-grounded generation (**2020**).
slides.notes: ⏱ 9:04:30 · 1 min — Do not read the table. One sentence: four communities added four signals to the same operation, and embeddings later gave them one representation. Point at Salton as the hinge.
slides.summary: answers: How has the historical development of IR, search, recommender systems and conversational interfaces? Cite Salton 1968 vector space model limitations.

slides.title: Learning to rank added a learned ordering layer
slides.body:
**Classical retrieval: BM25 + cosine similarity**

![[fig-bm25-cosine|105%]]

`score(q,d) = α · BM25(q,d) + (1 − α) · cosine(q,d)`, with hand-set `α ∈ [0,1]`.

> Pointwise linear regression learns feature weights; it cannot rerank documents omitted from the BM25 top-*k* set.

<!-- col -->

**Pointwise learning to rank: linear regression**

![[fig-pointwise-linear-regression]]

`ŷ(q,d) = w₀ + Σᵢ wᵢxᵢ(q,d)`; fit `w` from query–document relevance labels using squared error.

<!-- col -->

| | Classical | Pointwise LTR |
|---|---|---|
| Inputs | BM25 and cosine similarity | BM25, cosine similarity, and other query–document features |
| Weights | Hand-set `α` | Learned coefficients `wᵢ` |
| Output | Combined similarity score | Predicted relevance `ŷ(q,d)` |
| Scope | Retrieves and sorts documents | Reranks the BM25 top-*k* candidates |
slides.notes: ⏱ 9:05:30 · 2 min — Two stages: a cheap filter that must not miss, a learned ranker that orders. Trace the two columns, then the last line: a reranker cannot rescue what the first stage dropped.
slides.summary: answers: how learning to rank improved classical search .. show contrast of two retrieval pipelines - one works just with similarity on bm25 or tfidf, the second incorporated ML models trained in pointwise, pairwise or listwise settings

slides.title: The model is only half of learning to rank
slides.body:
**Scoring function**

`linear regression` → `regression trees (LambdaMART)` → `neural ranker`

<!-- gap -->

| Training objective | Training data | What it learns |
|---|---|---|
| **Itemwise cross-entropy** | `(query, document, relevant?)` | 1 relevance probability: `−y log p − (1−y) log(1−p)` |
| **Pairwise loss (RankNet)** | `(query, preferred doc, other doc)` | 1 score difference: `log(1 + exp(−(s⁺−s⁻)))` |
| **Listwise loss (ListNet)** | 1 query, its candidate list and graded labels | A distribution over the list via softmax cross-entropy |

**Pairwise loss computation — 4 animation steps**

`D⁺: "Noise-cancelling headphones, 30-hour battery"` → `D⁻: "Replacement headphone cable"` → `(D⁺, D⁻)` → `s⁺=1.2, s⁻=0.4` → `loss=log(1+exp(−0.8))=0.371`

<!-- col -->

![[fig-pairwise-loss-computation]]

> One pair supervises 1 score difference between 2 documents; it does not identify absolute relevance probabilities.
slides.notes: ⏱ 9:07:30 · 1½ min — Labels decide what the model can learn. Read the training-data column, not the formulas; mention that click labels carry position bias. If behind, skip the worked example.
slides.summary: of course linear regression can be replaced by something much more sophisticated, for example with regression trees or neural nets ... also depends which data are available for training - explain pairwise, listwise and cross entropy loss

slides.title: Transformers in search
slides.body:
<!-- gap -->

**Two ways to use [Transformer](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762) outputs for ranking**

<!-- gap -->

|  | Ranking Transformer | ColBERT |
|---|---|---|
| Encoder input | Query and document together | Query and document separately |
| Output used | One relevance score, often from `[CLS]` | One contextual vector per token |
| Interaction | Full attention inside the encoder | Late interaction after encoding |

> ColBERT retains token-level matching while moving document encoding out of the query path.

<!-- col -->

![[fig-colbert-maxsim-pipeline|105%]]
slides.notes: ⏱ 9:09 · 1½ min — Cross-encoder: accurate, unsearchable. ColBERT: encode documents in advance, compare tokens at query time. Say the pattern — precompute the catalogue, keep the per-request work small.
slides.summary: Lets explain Colbert here, introduce transformer and ranking transformer, add image explaining internal structure and how outputs are used

slides.title: Search became a personalized retrieval problem
slides.body:
**Two neural signals**

- **Query relevance:** [ColBERT, 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.12832) matches neural query and document token embeddings.
- **User preference:**  learns neural item and user embeddings from interaction histories (sequences of item attributes).

![[fig-shared-user-embedding-search-recsys|68%]]

**Combined score**

`score(u,q,d) = ColBERT(q,d) + λ·cos(E_user(u), E_doc(d))`, Select `λ` on a held-out set for each retrieval task.

- [Bridging Language and Items for Retrieval and Recommendation: Benchmarking LLMs as Semantic Encoders](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.03952)
- [Alipay deployment](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3583780.3614657)

> Search ranks for a query `q`; personalization adds neural similarity between user `u` and document `d`.
slides.notes: ⏱ 9:10:30 · 1½ min — The convergence claim made concrete: one user vector, search adds a query term. Name Alipay and BLaIR as proof at two scales. Say it holds for logged-in product search, not the public web.
slides.summary: answers: How search went personalized and blended with recsys? Show diagram of shared user embedding space.

slides.title: A query is now a hypothesis about intent
slides.body:
![[fig-semantic-query-pipeline|68%]]

| Step | What the system computes | Named mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| **Complete** | Candidate continuations from the typed prefix, locale and session | [seq2seq, 2014](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.3215) or [Transformer](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762) next-token prediction |
| **Understand** | Contextual representation of intent, entities and constraints | Transformer encoder; [word2vec](https://arxiv.org/abs/1301.3781) is the earlier static-vector baseline |
| **Retrieve** | Lexical candidates plus semantic matches between query and items | [BM25, 1994](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/okapi-at-trec-3/) + [ColBERT, 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.12832) |
| **Answer** | Response conditioned on retrieved evidence rather than model memory alone | [RAG, 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401) |

> Search no longer matches a string; it predicts intent, retrieves evidence and composes an answer or ranked list of items.
slides.notes: ⏱ 9:12 · 1½ min — A search box is a chain of predictions: what you meant, what matches, what to say. Keep hybrid retrieval in the picture — BM25 still catches exact terms. The last step opens the conversational part.
slides.summary: answers: How search went semantic ... Search becomes semantic as users expect reasoning AI answering ... how semantic query understanding is done, how query prediction or completition is done ...

slides.title: LLM inference is constrained by memory and scheduling
slides.body:
[Transformer inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762) has two phases: **prefill** processes prompt tokens in parallel; **decode** generates one token per sequential model step.

| Constraint | Scaling | Serving effect |
|---|---|---|
| Model weights | parameters × bytes/parameter | [Llama 2 70B](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.09288) requires ≈140 GB for BF16 weights, excluding runtime buffers |
| KV cache | layers × active tokens × KV width | Llama 2 70B uses ≈320 KiB/token in BF16: ≈1.25 GiB per 4,096-token request |
| Prefill attention | $O(L^2)$ compute for sequence length $L$ | [FlashAttention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.14135) reduces memory traffic, not quadratic attention FLOPs |
| Decode | one sequential step per output token | Larger batches improve throughput but increase queueing and tail latency; [Orca](https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi22/presentation/yu) schedules at iteration granularity |
| Variable sequence lengths | fragmented KV-cache allocation | [PagedAttention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.06180) reports 2–4× higher throughput than FasterTransformer and Orca at comparable latency |

> For Llama 2 70B in BF16, one 4,096-token request adds ≈1.25 GiB of KV cache on top of ≈140 GB of weights.

<!-- col -->

***

![[fig-inference-memory-scheduling|92%]]

<!-- col -->

**Limits of common mitigations**

- 4-bit weights reduce the ideal 70B weight footprint from ≈140 GB to ≈35 GB; [GPTQ](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.17323) adds quantization error and kernel constraints.
- [Speculative decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.17192) reduces target-model decode steps, but gains depend on draft-model acceptance.
- Continuous batching raises utilization; latency still depends on arrival rate, output length and service-level targets.
slides.notes: ⏱ 9:13:30 · 1½ min — Arithmetic, not benchmarks: 140 GB of weights, 1.25 GiB of cache per long request, one sequential step per token. Name the four mitigations and their limits. If behind, say only the three numbers.

slides.title: Structure can beat parameter count on the right task
slides.body:
<!-- gap -->

| Result | Source |
|---|---|
| A **0.6 B** model with a semantic-ID encoder outperforms a **4 B** model without one on SID prediction; deepest-level accuracy improves **46% relative** | [PrefixMem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.00324), Pinterest 2026 |
| A sparse inverted-index retriever from the same BERT slightly beats its dense sibling: **0.322 vs 0.312 MRR@10** | [SPLADE](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.05720), 2021 |
| CompresSAE projects dense embeddings into a high-dimensional sparse space: **12× fewer parameters** at near-uncompressed quality, with sparse-space and reconstructed-dense inference modes | [CompresSAE](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.11388), RecSys 2025 |

<!-- gap -->

> CompresSAE stores active coordinates and values instead of every dense coordinate; it reconstructs a dense vector when required. [Kasalický et al., 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.11388)

<!-- col -->

![[fig-compressae-architecture]]

*CompresSAE architecture: [Kasalický et al., RecSys 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.11388).*

<!-- gap -->

**Illustrative representation of one item**, values are schematic:

| Form | Example |
|---|---|
| Original dense, `d=8` | `[0.18, -0.42, 0.07, 0.31, -0.09, 0.55, 0.12, -0.26]` |
| Sparse code, `D=16`, **3 active** | `{2: 0.81, 9: 0.34, 14: 0.22}`; the other **13** coordinates are `0` |
| Reconstructed dense, `d=8` | `[0.17, -0.40, 0.08, 0.30, -0.08, 0.53, 0.13, -0.25]` |
slides.notes: ⏱ 9:15 · 1½ min — Structure over parameters on the right task: 0.6B beats 4B with the right encoder; sparse matches dense; CompresSAE gives 12× fewer parameters with a speed/exactness dial. Read the first and last row.
slides.summary: Evidence from three places that structure buys more than parameters: a 0.6-billion model with a semantic-ID encoder beats a 4-billion one without; sparse retrievers match dense; CompresSAE cuts parameters twelvefold.

slides.title: Recommenders learn what matters to each user
slides.body:
![[fig-neural-recommender-flow|52%]]

| Signal | Core idea | Works when | Main limit |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Content-based** | Match item attributes to a user profile | New items have text, image, or metadata | Repeats what the user already consumed |
| **Collaborative filtering** | Learn from user–item interactions | Many users reveal shared preference patterns | Cold-start users and items |
| **Neural hybrid** | Embed history, items, and context; retrieve candidates, then rank | Large catalogs need multi-signal personalization | Serving requires memory and scheduling control |

<!-- col -->

> Recommendation is retrieval conditioned on a person.
slides.notes: ⏱ 9:16:30 · 1½ min — Content says what an item is, behaviour what people do with it. Read the 'works when' column. Land on: recommendation is retrieval conditioned on a person.
slides.summary: introduce recommender systems, content based, collaborative filterring, visual example of neural recommender

slides.title: User-based collaborative filtering: borrow votes from similar users
slides.body:
![[fig-user-cf-four-step|92%]]

| 1 · Observe | 2 · Compare | 3 · Aggregate | 4 · Recommend |
|---|---|---|---|
| User–item interactions | Find users with similar histories | Weight their scores by similarity | Rank items the target user has not seen |

**Prediction:** target-user baseline + similarity-weighted neighbour opinions
**Limit:** sparse histories and new users produce weak neighbourhoods ([GroupLens, 1994](https://doi.org/10.1145/192844.192905))

> People who agreed with you before become voters on what you may want next.
slides.notes: ⏱ 9:18 · 1½ min — Click through the four steps in the figure: matrix, neighbours, weighted votes, ranked item. Needs no item text; goes blind without history. If behind, skip the prediction formula.
slides.summary: explain user based collaborative fillering by animating the process step by step

slides.title: You cannot edit your own vector in recommender systems
slides.body:
| How you steer a recommender today | What it touches |
|---|---|
| Filters, boosters, business rules | the candidate list, after scoring |
| Prompting an LLM recommender ([P5](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.13366), 2022) | the text interface; collaborative signal is weak in warm catalogues |
| Instruction over semantic IDs ([GLIDE](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.17540), 2026) | the generator, at Spotify scale |
| Profile editors, explicit likes, critiquing | the interface again; the learned representation is untouched |
| **Changing the user embedding itself** | the model's internal state — the subject of the next three slides |

<!-- gap -->

> Existing controls sit outside the learned user representation. The question: can a sentence edit that representation directly?
slides.notes: ⏱ 9:22 · 1 min — Every control today acts around the model's picture of you, not on it. Ask the question and move on: can a sentence edit the vector directly?
slides.summary: Q4 opener: every recommender represents the user as a vector nobody can read or change; the ways to steer so far sit on top of the model, not inside it.

slides.title: LLM as a recommender: A language model is not a catalogue
slides.body:
![[fig-fluent-phantom-item]]

<!-- col -->

| LLM as RecSys | Production failure |
|---|---|
| Generates a plausible title | No matching item ID |
| Recalls facts from parameters | Stale price, availability, or policy |
| Sees only the prompt | Misses user history if not included in the prompt |
| Uses no collaborative-filtering system | Cannot use behaviour from similar users ([Koren et al., 2009](https://doi.org/10.1109/MC.2009.263)) |
| Generates candidates token by token | Adds LLM generation latency and bypasses recommender retrieval |
| Explains before validation | Fluent rationale hides the error |
| Handles the whole request | No behavioural ranking or business rules |

***

<!-- col -->

**Solution**:

Separate the jobs so LLM interprets → recommender retrieves and ranks valid IDs using catalogue, user-history and collaborative signals → LLM explains the returned items. This follows [RAG, 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401), with a recommender (not the language model) as the source of catalogue truth.

> Let the model choose the words—not invent the inventory.
slides.notes: ⏱ 9:23 · 2 min — Hallucination here means an item that does not exist. Walk the middle column briefly, then the fix: the model chooses words, the recommender owns the inventory. If behind, go straight to the solution column.
slides.summary: explain problems with conversational recommenation - talk to LLM ... halucinated items

slides.title: Unfold the vector: sparse autoencoders make a profile legible
slides.body:
- Train a collaborative-filtering backbone—ALS, ELSA, LightGCN, or two-tower—and separate `encode(interactions) → e` from `decode(e) → scores`.
- Fit a **TopK sparse autoencoder** to dense user embeddings: latent width = 2–8× the embedding width; ReLU; `k ∈ {16, 32}`.
- Learn a mapper from text embeddings to the SAE latent space using item metadata or synthetic requests.
- At inference, map a natural-language request, add its latent adjustment to the user’s sparse code, then run the SAE decoder and CF decoder.

![[fig-steering-pipeline|85%]]

**Reconstruction check:** At 4,096 latent dimensions, increasing `k` moves autoencoder-path NDCG toward backbone NDCG.

> MSc thesis of Jarda Hradil (2026)
slides.notes: ⏱ 9:27:30 · 1½ min — Sparse autoencoder unfolds the tangled user vector into a few named knobs; nothing is retrained. Say only the third bullet if behind. Credit Jarda Hradil's thesis.
slides.summary: Hradil 2026, part one: a TopK sparse autoencoder projects the dense CF user embedding into a wide latent where most features mean one thing.

slides.title: Say it: a sentence becomes a direction in that space
slides.body:
![[fig-steering-pipeline-2|68%]]

1. For every item, an LLM writes five short requests that describe it **without naming it** — *Toy Story* → "animated buddy adventure for all ages"; requests are split 3 / 1 / 1 per item into train, validation and test — so the test asks whether a **new phrasing** about a known item moves that item: paraphrase steering in an offline probe, not steering toward never-seen items. This closes the request–metadata gap the way HyDE closes the query–document gap in search.
2. A two-layer mapper learns text embedding (Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B) → the item's sparse code, trained with **InfoNCE** — a retrieval objective.
3. Online: embed the request, map it to a direction **δ**, normalise to the user's activation mass, then **blend** `(1−α)·user + α·δ` and re-apply TopK. Mass is normalised to avoid score-scale drift; the effect on ranking quality is measured, not assumed.
4. Decode through the SAE and the CF decoder → a steered ranking. No retraining anywhere.
slides.notes: ⏱ 9:29 · 2 min — A sentence becomes a direction in that space via search machinery — text embedder, InfoNCE, synthetic queries. Numbers: 24th → 3rd on MIND with ELSA; random request lowers the rank, so it is meaning, not mixing. State the limits: offline, exact-item probe, additive only.
slides.summary: Hradil 2026, part two: synthetic requests per item train a small mapper from text embeddings to the sparse latent; at inference the request is blended into the user's code with mass preserved.

slides.title: What a query costs at a hundred million users
slides.body:
![[fig-latency-budget|105%]]

<!-- col -->

| Constraint | Where it comes from |
|---|---|
| **> 400,000 requests per second, < 500 ms** | Kuaishou's stated envelope for its recommender ([OneRec report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.13695)) |
| **≈ 100 ms** end-to-end for a synchronous recommendation surface | an example product budget: retrieval, features, ranker, constraints and network share it |
| Thousands of tokens per request | what a language model costs when it is on the request path |

<!-- gap -->

Illustrative arithmetic (September 2026 list prices for a hosted model; self-hosting changes the number): 100 M users × 3 sessions × 5 pages = **1.5 billion ranking calls a day**. Put a language model on that path at 1,000 tokens a call and 10 cents per million tokens: **$150,000 a day** for the generation step alone, before retrieval, and before any cache hit. A dot product costs microseconds.
slides.notes: ⏱ 9:31 · 1½ min — One line of arithmetic: 1.5 billion ranking calls a day; a language model on that path is $150k a day before caching; a dot product is microseconds. Cost per request is an objective, not an ops detail.
slides.summary: Q6 opener: the budget nobody negotiates — QPS, latency, and the fact that a recommender request is a dot product while a language-model request is thousands of tokens.

slides.title: Compute versus value
slides.body:
<!-- gap -->

![[fig-scaling-laws]]

<!-- col -->

| | [HSTU](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.17152) (Meta, 2024) | [OneRec](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.13695) (Kuaishou, 2025) |
|---|---|---|
| Model change | 1.5 trillion parameters; "three orders of magnitude more computationally complex than prior state-of-the-art" — model complexity, not production cost | one end-to-end model replacing the cascade, ~10× its FLOPs |
| Business effect | "improve metrics in online A/B tests by 12.4 %" (metric not named) | App Stay Time +0.54 % / +1.24 % |
| Why it was affordable | M-FALCON amortises a 285× more complex model at 1.5–3× throughput | model-FLOPs utilisation 23.7 % / 28.8 % — the cascade had left the GPUs idle |

> In Kuaishou's accounting the saving came from using the hardware, not from a smarter model — and the migration cost is not in the report.
slides.notes: ⏱ 9:32:30 · 1½ min — HSTU: three orders of magnitude of model complexity for 12.4%. OneRec: ten times the arithmetic, a tenth of the cost, because the cascade left the GPUs idle. Migration cost is not in either report.
slides.summary: The scaling law arrived in recommendation, and so did its bill: Meta's HSTU paid three orders of magnitude of compute for +12.4 %; Kuaishou's OneRec paid ten times the FLOPs and a tenth of the money.

slides.title: Four serving levers
slides.body:
![[fig-serving-tricks|140%]]

<!-- col -->

| Lever | System | Reported effect |
|---|---|---|
| **Cache the user state across requests** (hierarchical KV cache, GPU + host RAM) | [MTServe](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.22881), 2026 | up to **3.1×** faster, hit ratio > 98.5 % |
| **Reuse the encoding across stages** (retrieval and ranking share one KV cache) | [UniPinRec](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.00422), Pinterest | > 3× ranking forward-pass speedup; −11.1 % latency |
| **Deduplicate attention** over the shared user sequence | [PinFM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.12704), Pinterest | **+600 %** serving throughput, +200 % training |
| **Linear attention + request-level batching** for 10,000-event histories | [Douyin](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.06077), 2026 | −77–84 % bandwidth; 10k histories at full traffic |

> At scale a modelling win is realised only together with a serving win. Read the systems section of these papers first.
slides.notes: ⏱ 9:34 · 1 min — The person's history is the expensive part of every request: cache it, share it between stages, never encode it twice. Read the first and last row; the rest is on the slide.
slides.summary: Q7: the tricks that make long histories and big models fit the budget — caches across requests, reuse across stages, deduplicated attention, linear attention with request-level batching.

slides.title: Linear models are not dead
slides.body:
![[fig-ease-vs-elsa|135%]]

<!-- col -->

| | [EASE](https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.03375) (Netflix, 2019) | **ELSA** (Recombee Labs, [RecSys 2022](https://doi.org/10.1145/3523227.3551482)) |
|---|---|---|
| Model | a dense item–item matrix, closed form, negatives allowed | the hidden layer factorised into low-rank plus sparse |
| Cost | O(items²) memory — ten million items squared at 32-bit is about 400 TB of weights | **O(items · d)** — the item–item matrix is never materialised |
| Accuracy | strongest simple baseline in the field | **beats EASE** on several tasks; industrial validation in ACM TORS 2025 |
| Where | MovieLens | production, catalogues of tens of millions of items; successor **SANSA** deployed |

> Keep a strong linear baseline, stupid.
slides.notes: ⏱ 9:35 · 1½ min — EASE is the strongest simple baseline and needs a 400 TB matrix; ELSA factorises it, scales linearly and is more accurate — ours, RecSys 2022, in production. Keep a strong linear baseline.
slides.summary: EASE was the strongest simple baseline and could not be deployed; ELSA made it scale and beat it; SANSA runs it in production.

slides.group: Our Transformers and multimodal foundational models
slides.title: beeFormer: interaction data inside the text encoder
slides.body:
<!-- gap -->

![[fig-beeformer|90%]]

<!-- col -->

> ELSA stopped being only a model. It became a loss function you can use to train something else entirely.

<!-- gap -->

- A sentence Transformer ([Sentence-BERT](https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.10084) lineage) encodes item text; the **ELSA** objective reconstructs users' interaction vectors through the item–item operator; the gradient reaches the encoder.
- One encoder whose vectors understand both what an item **is** and what people **do** with it: cold-start and zero-shot, and transfer across domains — train on books, recommend films.
- Training on several domains accumulates knowledge in one model. Open source: [github.com/recombee/beeformer](https://github.com/recombee/beeformer) · paper [arXiv:2409.10309](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.10309).
slides.notes: ⏱ 9:36:30 · 1 min — beeFormer: let the recommendation loss flow into the text encoder, so it learns what people do, not just what things are called. Ours, RecSys 2024, open source.
slides.summary: RecSys 2024: let the recommendation loss — ELSA — flow back into a sentence Transformer, so one encoder reads both text and behaviour.

slides.group: Our Transformers and multimodal foundational models
slides.title: Our REEF protocol, evaluation of recsys foundational models
slides.body:
![[fig-winning-config]]

<!-- col -->

<!-- gap -->

| Recall@10, frozen → fine-tuned (BGE-M3 + SigLIP2) | Standard | Cold start |
|---|---|---|
| MovieLens 20M | 0.301 → 0.349 (**+15.9 %**) | +13.7 % |
| H&M Fashion | 0.164 → 0.211 (**+28.7 %**) | +23.4 % |
| Amazon Reviews 2023 | 0.121 → 0.154 (**+27.3 %**) | **+39.0 %** |

<!-- gap -->

- **LoRA** beats full fine-tuning everywhere; on Amazon full fine-tuning is *worse than the frozen encoder* (0.121 → 0.115).
- **ELSA** beats BPR, InfoNCE, Jaccard and PMI as the objective; ELSA + InfoNCE together collapse (0.323 → 0.245).
- **Honest negative:** four of six cross-domain and cross-dataset transfer settings stay at the random-ranker floor.

> Master thesis of Tomáš Laurin (2026)
slides.notes: ⏱ 9:37:30 · 1½ min — REEF: hold everything still, vary only the encoder. Read the table: frozen → fine-tuned, +16–29%, cold start +39% on Amazon; LoRA beats full fine-tuning; the winning objective is the 2022 linear loss. Say the negative result: transfer mostly failed. Credit Tomáš Laurin's thesis. Bridge: cheaper stack, more power per ranking decision — alignment next.
slides.summary: Laurin 2026, fine-tuning multimodal encoders on interactions under REEF: LoRA + interaction-conditioned attention fusion + ELSA wins; full fine-tuning damages the pretrained space; transfer mostly fails.

slides.title: Alignment is a table of measurable properties
slides.body:
| Property | The question | Metric | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Controllable** | can the user move it where they want? | rank of the requested item (MRR) | natural-language steering of the user embedding |
| **Safe** | what does it let through, leak or do? | harmful-query accuracy; leakage and policy tests | moderation + retrieval filtering + output and action constraints + audit |
| **Fair exposure** | who gets seen? | exposure share of items and suppliers | minimum-exposure guarantees, re-ranking |
| **Calibrated** | does my 4 mean your 4? | rating-level consistency across users | user-specific discretisation of a shared semantic scale |
| **Evaluable** | is the judge better than the proxy? | correlation with A/B outcomes | behaviourally aligned judges and simulators |

> Every row is engineering: a number to move, a component that moves it.
slides.notes: ⏱ 9:39 · 1 min — Alignment as five measurable properties, each with a metric and a component. Read the property column only; the next slides are the rows.
slides.summary: Q8 opener: for an engineer, alignment is not a model's mood; it is five properties, each with a metric and a mechanism, each with a production example.

slides.title: Convergence merges vulnerabilities: SHIELD
slides.body:
![[fig-shield|105%]]

**SHIELD** (Recombee Labs, UMAP 2025): hierarchical LLM-generated queries → reward-model filtering → classifier. Marketplace evaluation, 17,170 harmful and 8,871 sensitive queries:

<!-- col -->

| Accuracy on the marketplace test set | BM25 keyword similarity | Semantic embeddings + FAISS | **MoralBERT, fine-tuned** |
|---|---|---|---|
| harmful vs. sensitive queries | 93.2 % | 96.5 % | **98.4 %** (F1 98.6 %) |

> Merge the stacks and you merge the attack surface. The fix has to understand meaning as well as the search does.
slides.notes: ⏱ 9:40 · 1 min — Semantic search walked around the keyword filter — 'glass tubing'. SHIELD: generated queries, reward-model filter, classifier, 98.4%. Ours, UMAP 2025.
slides.summary: Semantic search understands meaning, so harmful queries walk around keyword filters; SHIELD is the dataset and classifier that closes the gap.

slides.title: Exposure and the feedback loop
slides.body:
![[fig-feedback-loop|105%]]

<!-- col -->

| Finding | Source |
|---|---|
| A recommend → click → retrain loop amplifies popularity bias, shrinks catalogue coverage and homogenises profiles; the minority user group loses most precision | Mansoury, PhD thesis 2021 ([arXiv:2111.05564](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.05564)) |
| Seven named biases enter at three points — data, model, results — and the loop feeds them back | [Chen et al., bias and debias survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.03240) |
| Web-search diversification (xQuAD) and fair top-k ranking reused as recommender re-rankers | same thesis — the post-processing slot is shared across interfaces |
| **Minimum item exposure guarantees**: eligible items get an exposure floor, with a measured relevance trade-off | Recombee Labs, 2024 — [blog](https://www.recombee.com/blog/making-recommendations-fairer-a-new-way-to-guarantee-exposure-for-all) |
slides.notes: ⏱ 9:41 · ½ min — The model learns only from what it showed; the loop amplifies popularity and hurts minority users most. Exposure is a resource — put a floor under it (ours, with a measured trade-off). Half a minute.
slides.summary: The model learns only from what it showed; the loop amplifies popularity, shrinks coverage and hurts minority users most; exposure guarantees are the engineering answer.

slides.title: Evaluation is alignment: judges need behavioural alignment too
slides.body:
**Bidirectional rationalisation** ([Ziabari et al., 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11493)): in zero-shot, an LLM "convincingly argues for both positive and negative user engagement outcomes on the exact same item with identical evidence".

| Judge | MacroF1 on real homepage interaction logs |
|---|---|
| zero-shot LLM | baseline |
| behaviourally aligned LLM (fine-tuning + preference optimisation over paired rationales) | **+32.19 %**, matches the production feature-engineered model |

A simulator earns trust the same way: ContextSim is checked against 55 real A/B experiments, not against its own plausibility.

> A judge that can argue either way is not a judge. Align it to behaviour, then measure the correlation.

<!-- col -->

![[fig-circular-evaluation|130%]]
slides.notes: ⏱ 9:41:30 · ½ min — A zero-shot LLM judge argues both ways on the same evidence; aligned to behaviour it matches the production model. Anything between offline and A/B must be calibrated against real outcomes. Half a minute.
slides.summary: Off-the-shelf LLM judges argue convincingly for both outcomes on the same evidence; fine-tuning with preference optimisation over correct and counterfactual rationales fixes it and matches a production feature baseline.

slides.title: The rules outside the model
slides.body:
| Rule | What it asks of a recommender | Which slide answers it |
|---|---|---|
| **DSA, Article 27** | state the main parameters of the recommender system in plain language, and let users influence them | Controllable — steering by language |
| **DSA, Article 38** | very large platforms must offer at least one option not based on profiling | Exposure guarantees; a non-personalised ranking path |
| **AI Act, Article 50** | transparency obligations for AI-generated content | Grounding — cited evidence; audit trail |

> Regulation is arriving as a list of properties. The engineering table four slides ago is the same list.
slides.notes: ⏱ 9:42 · ½ min — DSA 27 and 38, AI Act 50 — the regulator's list is the engineering table from slide 27. No dates on the slide; drop this slide entirely if behind.
slides.summary: Two European obligations turn alignment properties into requirements: the DSA asks recommenders to explain their main parameters and offer user control; the AI Act adds transparency duties for generated content.

slides.title: The fourth interface: the consumer of the ranking changes
slides.body:
![[fig-agentic-protocols|90%]]

| What changed | What did not |
|---|---|
| Five agent-commerce protocols in nine months; the pattern settling on *discover in the chat, transact on the merchant site* | the catalogue still has to be retrieved from, ranked and constrained |
| Structured attributes and current inventory make items easier for an agent to retrieve, compare and safely transact | the winner is still the best-ranked item — for a new kind of requester |

> Search, recommendation, conversation — and now an agent asks the same question on the user's behalf.
slides.notes: ⏱ 9:42:30 · 1 min — Agents are a new client of the same stack, not a new stack. Say the last row: structured catalogues are what agents can act on — Klímek's keynote from inside the product; constrained decoding is Mannaert's guard rail. Skip the protocol race if behind.
slides.summary: Q9: for the first time the entity reading the ranked list is not a person but an agent acting on a person's behalf; the ranking job is the same, the requester is new.

slides.title: Four threads, one question
slides.body:
![[fig-portfolio|60%]]

| Axis | Flagship | One result |
|---|---|---|
| **Accuracy** | REEF — compare encoders with everything else held still | in one protocol, a frozen encoder plus LoRA and the ELSA loss: Recall@10 +16–29 % |
| **Affordability** | ELSA and CompresSAE — linear and sparse by design | linear cost, more accurate than EASE; embeddings with 12× fewer parameters |
| **Alignment** | SHIELD and language steering — safety and control as numbers | 98.4 % harmful-query accuracy; the requested item from ≈ 24th to ≈ 3rd |

> Frontier labs work on being better. We have spent ten years on being good enough within a budget somebody will approve. That is a different question — and it is the one more people have.
slides.notes: ⏱ 9:43:30 · 1 min — The portfolio on the three axes — everything here was already used as evidence. End on the sentence: good enough within a budget somebody will approve is a different question, and the one more people have.
slides.summary: Every publication answers one question: how to get large-model quality into a budget an ordinary company can approve.

slides.title: Where this goes: controllable, evaluable, safe ... and perhaps agentic ...
slides.body:
![[fig-whats-next|120%]]

Conversational recommender systems that are **controllable, evaluable, and safe**."

<!-- col -->

<!-- gap -->

| Word | What it already means here |
|---|---|
| **controllable** | steering by language (Hradil), constrained decoding, business rules as a query language |
| **evaluable** | REEF, offline-to-online correlation, behaviourally aligned judges |
| **safe** | SHIELD, exposure guarantees, an agent interface that cannot ask about another user |

<!-- gap -->

> Recommender system and reasoning agents in agent2agent online marketplaces.
slides.notes: ⏱ 9:44:30 · ½ min — Controllable, evaluable, safe: each already has a working component; the two theses are the first steps. One sentence on agent-to-agent marketplaces, then thank you.
slides.summary: The lab's direction for 2026 in our Head of Research's words, and how each word maps to something already shown.

<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="2 2 797 326" width="800" height="330" role="img" aria-label="Conversational requests are interpreted by an LLM, converted into preferences, ranked against the Recombee catalogue, and rendered only when backed by returned catalogue IDs.">
  <rect width="797" height="326" fill="#FAFAF7" x="2" y="2"></rect>
  <defs>
    <marker id="arrow-purple" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="8.5" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto">
      <path d="M0 0L10 5L0 10Z" fill="#7C3AED"></path>

    <marker id="arrow-green" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="8.5" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto">
      <path d="M0 0L10 5L0 10Z" fill="#10B981"></path>
    </marker>
    <style>
      text { font-family: Inter, ui-sans-serif, system-ui, sans-serif; }
      .flowDot { animation: flow 6s ease-in-out infinite; }
      .gatePulse { transform-box: fill-box; transform-origin: center; animation: gate 6s ease-in-out infinite; }
      .blockedPulse { animation: blocked 6s ease-in-out infinite; }
      @keyframes flow {
        0%, 10%, 100% { transform: translateX(0); opacity: .45; }
        42%, 58% { transform: translateX(22px); opacity: 1; }
      }
      @keyframes gate {
        0%, 55%, 100% { transform: scale(1); }
        68% { transform: scale(1.04); }
      }
      @keyframes blocked {

<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 800 450" font-family="system-ui,sans-serif">

  <rect class="choice1" x="30" y="70" width="230" height="222" rx="10" fill="#D1FAE5" stroke="#065F46" stroke-width="2"></rect>

    <tspan x="145" dy="27" font-size="17" font-weight="700" fill="#065F46">LoRA ✓</tspan>
    <tspan x="145" dy="29" font-size="11" font-weight="700" fill="#6B7280">MECHANISM</tspan>
    <tspan x="145" dy="20">Low-rank Δ learns; backbone fixed</tspan>
    <tspan x="145" dy="19" fill="#065F46">Pretrained geometry is preserved</tspan>
    <tspan x="145" dy="27" font-size="11" font-weight="700" fill="#991B1B">FIXES FULL-TUNE FAILURE</tspan>
    <tspan x="145" dy="20" fill="#991B1B">Full tuning can damage</tspan>
    <tspan x="145" dy="18" fill="#991B1B">the pretrained geometry</tspan>
  </text>

  <text x="400" y="92" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11.5" fill="#1E1B4B">
    <tspan x="400" font-size="11" font-weight="700" fill="#6B7280">FUSION</tspan>
    <tspan x="400" dy="25" font-size="15" font-weight="700" fill="#065F46">Interaction-conditioned</tspan>
    <tspan x="400" dy="19" font-size="15" font-weight="700" fill="#065F46">attention ✓</tspan>
    <tspan x="400" dy="25" font-size="11" font-weight="700" fill="#6B7280">MECHANISM</tspan>
    <tspan x="400" dy="20">αᵢ·text + (1−αᵢ)·image</tspan>
    <tspan x="400" dy="19" fill="#065F46">The weight is learned per item</tspan>
    <tspan x="400" dy="24" font-size="11" font-weight="700" fill="#991B1B">FIXES INDEPENDENT ENCODERS</tspan>
    <tspan x="400" dy="19" fill="#991B1B">Text and image need not share</tspan>
    <tspan x="400" dy="18" fill="#991B1B">one calibrated relevance scale</tspan>

  <rect x="350" y="308" width="100" height="18" rx="6" fill="#FAFAF7" stroke="none"></rect>
